game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the title might imply a heavy-handed narrative (and that's not entirely unfair of a criticism of the game itself), this one impressed me more than I thought a simple concept would. 

The idea is simple. There's been a bombing, and you are entrusted with a spy program that allows you to pry into the personal lives of several suspects, making new connections as you dig up their conversations and posts. You'll be listening in on phone calls, scanning private messages and texts, and figuring out aliases all in hopes of preventing another attack. The morally dubious circumstances are obvious throughout but there's plenty of player choice to determine just how you use a tool of such power.

The way it works is as you read, bits of information flagged as "important" by the program will automatically be highlighted. The twist is that only you can see the context of that information. Once uploaded to your supervisor, it will be taken at strictly face value, no questions asked. This makes no sense at all of course, but just roll with it. So while it would be easy to just upload everything you see, the branching story will turn out much more negatively for everyone involved as a result. 

And you will probably care, too. The characters you're tasked with spying on are all realistically flawed and well-written. You might find yourself getting invested in their lives and relationships as you spend more and more time spying on them, and might even feel motivated to protect them. The classic "will you obey your superiors?" question that comes up in these kinds of games (see also: Papers, Please and etc) is done well and can have serious consequences for how things turn out for each person. Whether it's leaving out something incriminating, or simply ensuring that you don't upload anything out of context, or making a difficult decision between two conflicting bits of information. 

It's a good story, even if it paints its themes of authoritarianism and rebellion in broad, easy strokes, and your personal experience with it will vary depending on a lot of factors. There are some good twists and plenty of believable dialogue. While the concept is far-fetched and sometimes difficult to believe, it's executed well enough that I was sucked into its world for the few hours of entertainment I got out of it. No regrets.

The way it works is as you read, bits of information flagged as "important" by the program will automatically be highlighted. The twist is that only you can see the context of that information. Once uploaded to your supervisor, it will be taken at strictly face value, no questions asked. This makes no sense at all of course, but just roll with it. So while it would be easy to just upload everything you see, the branching story will turn out much more negatively for everyone involved as a result. And you will probably care, too. The characters you're tasked with spying on are all realistically flawed and well-written. You might find yourself getting invested in their lives and relationships as you spend more and more time spying on them, and might even feel motivated to protect them. The classic "will you obey your superiors?" question that comes up in these kinds of games (see also: Papers, Please and etc) is done well and can have serious consequences for how things turn out for each person. Whether it's leaving out something incriminating, or simply ensuring that you don't upload anything out of context, or making a difficult decision between two conflicting bits of information. It's a good story, even if it paints its themes of authoritarianism and rebellion in broad, easy strokes, and your personal experience with it will vary depending on a lot of factors. There are some good twists and plenty of believable dialogue. While the concept is far-fetched and sometimes difficult to believe, it's executed well enough that I was sucked into its world for the few hours of entertainment I got out of it. No regrets.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that has motivated me to take the time to write a review again, something I have not done in a while.  I'll admit, the title using the name of the author of a favorite book of mine grabbed my attention, and the description of the gameplay was enough to get me to take the plunge during the winter sale.  What followed was several hours spent parsing through the personal data of a group of fictional persons to solve the mystery of a terror attack and to consider the tradeoffs between privacy and security.

Let me start by saying that Orwell is at no point pedantic.  On the very rare occassion a character has been preachy, it was entirley in character for an activist.  This game has you violating privacy in order to achieve a verifiable and practical good; if you are a successful investigator you can literally save lives.  I'd do a diservice to potential players though to say any more than the very vague and cliche question of "At what cost?"

The gameplay is surprisingly interesting and reminded me is a lot of ways of the surprise hit "Papers, Please."  In the not-to-distant future The Party has enacted a new security measure that gathers every scrap of digital information a person could leave.  However, to address internal privacy concerns no one person sees everything and makes decisions.  You play an "Investigator" who has been hired to comb through relevant data as determined by the search algorythims of the Orwell system.  As you read people's emails, chatlogs, and visit their blogs and social media sites you decide what information to pass onto your Advisor.  His role is to determine who merits investigation and draw conclusions from the data you send.  That is to say, the only information the insider in law enforcement is allowed to see is what you deem relevant.  To do your job well you must avoid not only missing relevant data, but oversharing data that could be taken out of context or is irrelevant.  Of course, since it is completley up to you to decide what is relevant, this opens the door to different investigation outcomes I fully intend to explore in future playthroughs, even if I do know the answer to the mystery.

The mystery is also quite enthralling.  I write this review at 3AM, having completed the game in a single sitting of several hours, sucked in by the need to uncover "just one more" piece of the puzzle until suddenly I was furiously not only trying to solve the whole riddle, but making ethical considerations over what I should share or if I should continue to do my job "properly."  If you enjoy a good mystery or if you like very interactive VN-style games like Analogue: A Hate Story (which I also reccomend), then I can't tell you to buy this quickly enough, even if it isn't on sale.  This was a unique and wonderful gaming experience that I am glad I had.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
For the four and half hours I spent playing this game, I also occupied myself with watching television or movies. This is probably reasonably reflective of what I would do if I was one of these investigators in real life.

Orwell isn’t the most engaging of games in terms gameplay. It’s a simple task of continually dragging and dropping tidbits of information into the Orwell system so that it can compile the profiles and allow your “handler” to make assessments about the next course of engagement. Sometimes you have to choose between conflicting bits of information, but other than that, there’s generally little reason to not put information in the system as you come across it, except maybe to avoid your handler’s smart-arse remarks.

Orwell is a far more engaging game in terms of the ideas it presents and the world it builds. As I am sure you have guessed, Orwell derives heavily from the ideas put forward 1984 by George Orwell. Similarly to 1984, Orwell is set in a fictional country where media and many other outlets are controlled by the government. That being said, the Nation in which the game is set is more of an authoritarian society as opposed to full totalitarian.

By the time the ending rolled around, I was surprised by its direction. I mostly expected a “twist” where you are betrayed and would have to fight the government you were working for. But there was nothing quite that overt or direct, as you were presented with several opportunities with how to proceed. It was an interesting enough story built inside a world into which a lot of effort had been poured into its construction.

Orwell is not a thriller or a game that will keep you in suspense. Instead, it is a quiet and simple exploration of an old idea through a different lens, done tastefully and staying far enough away from the usual tropes to retain some uniqueness.

review_text_raw:
"Big Brother has arrived - and it’s you." In Orwell, you are tasked to report to the government on potential threats. You use the all powerful Orwell spying software to gleam every bit of info from any deemed suspicious. The catch is that you work with a supervisor who can speak to you, but you cannot speak to them. The only thing the supervisor sees from you are the snippets of information you send them, so you have to be careful that what you send will not be taken out of context.

Orwell is an interactive story, where your choices matter. The entire story is told through text and images, there is no voice acting. If you like text adventure games/interactive fiction or choose-your-own-adventure books, you will like this game, you'll also enjoy it if you want to feel like a detective piecing together clues. If you don't like reading, this is not the game for you. It's hard to compare this game to another because the gameplay is rather unique. I came into this game from Stories Untold and Event[0] looking for more games that tell a story and require you to think, and I was not disappointed.

[h1]“It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.”[/h1]
Set in [strike]America[/strike] [i][b]the Nation[/b][/i] in April, 2017, Orwell places you in the shoes of a newly hired Investigator, employees of the government whose jobs are to sift through and find information online to upload to Orwell, a new surveillance system currently being tested in the Nation. Your job begins after a bomb detonates in a busy city, prompting a search to uncover the group behind the attack. You become responsible for thwarting more attacks, unmasking the activist group Thought, and eventually determining the future of the Nation for years to come.

[h1]“He who controls the past controls the future. He who controls the present controls the past.”[/h1]
A terrifying piece of gameplay is the ability to write the narrative. A man comments in one place that he never wanted to harm anyone, while in another message, he expresses his satisfaction about recent events. To an extent, you are given the choice of deciding what Orwell and the Government learn about people.
Orwell is very obviously supposed to reference the situation beginning to develop in America right now, with whistleblower revelations revealing many of the activities conducted by some government departments. Surveillance is an increasingly relevant issue to today's world, and Orwell puts you on the other side of the issue.
One of the questions the game asks is whether or not the ends justify the means. You will trample over the privacy of many people, getting into their email accounts, bank accounts, computers, phones, and even forum accounts. Your methods are undoubtedly illegal, and you have multiple chances to ruin lives as you go.

[h1]“Until they became conscious they will never rebel, and until after they have rebelled they cannot become conscious.”[/h1]
(There isn't really a relevant 1984 quote about the part below.)

As for gameplay, you're staring at Orwell's GUI the whole time. There is a browser on the right, and profiles on the left. You gain information by dragging pieces of data (highlighted blue, or yellow if conflicting with other data) onto the relevant profiles, with your advisor giving his two cents from time to time. The game requires a lot of reading to fully understand the story. Orwell isn't a game you rush through. It's similar to a Telltale game in the way that gameplay<narrative. You will have to dig through websites, hack into computer desktops, and listen to conversations. 

The game took me about 4 hours to complete, but left me thinking about its topics for a long time after I logged out.

The biggest fault I have with Orwell is that there is no voice acting. Scenes where you listen in on calls could become so much more powerful with a decent voice actor or two to really put emotion into the characters.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of. Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/-dAXOFIVEDw

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.
